arXiv:2209.01946v2 [math.AP] 02 Jan 2023

Exponential Synchronization of Memristive HIndmarsh-Rose Neural Networks

Yuncheng You Address: Professor Emeritus, University of South Florida, Tampa, FL 33620, USA Email address: you@mail.usf.edu
Date: January 2, 2023
Abstract.

A new model of neural networks in terms of the memristive Hindmarsh-Rose equations is proposed. Globally dissipative dynamics is shown with absorbing sets in the state spaces. Through sharp and uniform grouping estimates and by leverage of integral and interpolation inequalities tackling the linear network coupling against the memristive nonlineariry, it is proved that exponential synchronization at a uniform convergence rate occurs when the coupling strengths satisfy the threshold conditions which are quantitatively expressed by the parameters.

Key words and phrases: 
Memristive Hindmarsh-Rose equations, dissipative dynamics, exponential synchronization, coupling strength, neural network.
2010 Mathematics Subject Classification
35B40, 35B41, 35K55, 37L30, 92C20

1. Introduction

The diffusive Hindmarsh-Rose equations with memristors is a new model for single neuron dynamics proposed by this author very recently [36]. In this paper, we shall pursue the topic of synchronization of a neural network described by such a model of the memristive and diffusive Hindmarsh-Rose equations with linear couplings.

Consider a network of mm fully coupled neuron cells denoted by 𝒩𝒲={𝒩i:i=1,2,⋯,m}\mathcal{NW}=\{\mathcal{N}_{i}:i=1,2,\cdots,m\}, where m≥2m\geq 2 is a positive integer. We shall study the dynamics and the synchronization problem of the following mathematical model of this neural network. Each neuron 𝒩i\mathcal{N}_{i} in this network is described by the four differential equations

(1.1) ∂ui∂t=η1​Δ​ui+a​ui2−b​ui3+vi−wi+Je−k1​φ​(ρi)​ui+∑j=1mP⁡(uj−ui),∂vi∂t=α−β​ui2−vi,∂wi∂t=q⁡(ui−ue)−r​wi,∂ρi∂t=η2​Δ​ρi+ui−k2​ρi+∑j=1mQ⁡(ρj−ρi),\begin{split}\frac{\partial u_{i}}{\partial t}&=\eta_{1}\Delta u_{i}+au_{i}^{2}-bu_{i}^{3}+v_{i}-w_{i}+J_{e}-k_{1}\varphi(\rho_{i})u_{i}+\sum_{j=1}^{m}P(u_{j}-u_{i}),\\ \frac{\partial v_{i}}{\partial t}&=\alpha-\beta u_{i}^{2}-v_{i},\\[3.0pt] \frac{\partial w_{i}}{\partial t}&=q(u_{i}-u_{e})-rw_{i},\\[3.0pt] \frac{\partial\rho_{i}}{\partial t}&=\eta_{2}\Delta\rho_{i}+u_{i}-k_{2}\rho_{i}+\sum_{j=1}^{m}Q(\rho_{j}-\rho_{i}),\end{split}

for 1≤i≤m,t>0,x∈Ω⊂ℝn1\leq i\leq m,\;t>0,\;x\in\Omega\subset\mathbb{R}^{n} (n≤3n\leq 3), where Ω\Omega is a bounded domain with locally Lipschitz continuous boundary ∂Ω\partial\Omega. In the membrane potential uiu_{i}-equations for neuron 𝒩i\mathcal{N}_{i}, the quadratic nonlinear form

(1.2) φ(ρi)=c+γρi+δρi2,i=1,2,⋯,m.\varphi(\rho_{i})=c+\gamma\rho_{i}+\delta\rho_{i}^{2},\quad i=1,2,\cdots,m.

presents the memristive effect, where ρi​(t,x)\rho_{i}(t,x) stands for the memductance of the memristor and φ⁡(ρi)\varphi(\rho_{i}) is the the electromagnetic induction flux with its strength coefficient k1k_{1}. In this system (1.1), the variable ui​(t,x)u_{i}(t,x) refers to the membrane electrical potential of a neuron cell, the variable vi​(t,x)v_{i}(t,x) called the spiking variable represents the transport rate of the ions of sodium and potassium through the fast ion channels, and the variable wi​(t,x)w_{i}(t,x) called the bursting variable represents the transport rate across the neuron membrane through slow channels of calcium and other ions. From biological and mathematical perspectives, the network neuron coupling terms are assumed to be linear in the membrane potential equations and the memristor equations with the coupling strength coefficient PP and QQ respectively.

All the parameters a,b,η1,η2,α,β,q,r,δ,k1,k2,P,Qa,b,\eta_{1},\eta_{2},\alpha,\beta,q,r,\delta,k_{1},k_{2},P,Q and the external input JeJ_{e} can be any positive constants, while the reference membrane potential value ueu_{e} and the two parameters c,γc,\gamma of the memductance (1.2) can be any real number constants.

We impose the homogeneous Neumann boundary conditions

(1.3) ∂ui∂ν​(t,x)=0,∂ρi∂ν​(t,x)=0,for​t>0,x∈∂Ω,1≤i≤m.\frac{\partial u_{i}}{\partial\nu}(t,x)=0,\quad\frac{\partial\rho_{i}}{\partial\nu}(t,x)=0,\quad\text{for}\;\;t>0,\;x\in\partial\Omega,\quad 1\leq i\leq m.

The initial states of the system (1.1) will be denoted by

(1.4) ui0​(x)=ui​(0,x),vi0​(x)=vi​(0,x),wi0​(x)=wi​(0,x),ρi0=ρi​(0,x),  1≤i≤m.u_{i}^{0}(x)=u_{i}(0,x),\;v_{i}^{0}(x)=v_{i}(0,x),\;w_{i}^{0}(x)=w_{i}(0,x),\;\rho_{i}^{0}=\rho_{i}(0,x),\;\;1\leq i\leq m.

The original Hindmarsh-Rose neuron model [13] consists of three ordinary differential equations without memristors and it features characterization of the firing-bursting dynamics for neurons, which generates sophisticated Hopf bifurcations and semi-numerical analyses leading to many new solution patterns and collective synchronization behavior [4, 8, 9, 16, 17, 18, 21, 29, 33, 37], especially chaotic bursting dynamics, in comparison with the classical highly nonlinear Hodgkin-Huxley equations [14] and the two-dimensional FitzHugh-Nagumo equations [11].

Global dynamics and synchronization of ensemble neurons modeled by partly diffusive Hindmarsh-Rose equations have been studied by the author’s group in recent years [19, 20, 21, 22]. Such a model of hybrid PDE and ODE reflects the structural feature of neuron cells, which contain the short-branch dendrites receiving incoming signals and the long-branch axon propagating and transmitting outgoing signals through synapses.

The concept of so-called memristor was coined by Leon Chua [6] to denote the effect of electromagnetic flux on moving electric charges. General memristive systems [7] attracted broad scientific interests in the recent one and half decades since the seminal publication [28]. Memristors are recognized in many advanced neuron models and applications [1, 2, 3, 25, 30, 32, 34, 35] as a different type (other than electrical and chemical) synapsis which can carry dynamically memorized signal information.

The researches on memristive Hindmarsh-Rose neuron model of ODE have been richly expanding, cf. [1, 3, 4, 10, 23, 24, 27, 34] and many references therein. Results on synchronization with the memristive coupling in the ODE models are achieved [12, 15, 30, 31, 33, 35] mainly by the approaches of generalized Hamiltonian functions, Lyapunov exponents, with numerical simulations. However, it is not seen any reported synchronization results on the memristive-based diffusive neural networks modeled by hybrid differential equations.

In this work we shall rigorously prove a sufficient threshold condition only on the network coupling strengths PP and QQ to ensure an exponential synchronization of this proposed neural network with a uniform convergence rate, through the approach of dissipative dynamics analysis and the sharp uniform estimates. The methodology in this work can be extended to study more complex neural networks in a broad scope.

The global existence and uniqueness of the weak solutions and their continuous dependence on the initial data shown in Theorem 3.1 enable us to define the solution semiflow [26] of the memristive and diffusive Hindmarsh-Rose equations (1.1) on the space EE as follows:

S(t):g0⟼g(t;g0)=col(ui(t,⋅),vi(t,⋅),wi(t,⋅),ρi(t,⋅):1≤i≤m),t≥0.S(t):g_{0}\longmapsto g(t;g_{0})=\text{col}\,(u_{i}(t,\cdot),v_{i}(t,\cdot),w_{i}(t,\cdot),\rho_{i}(t,\cdot):1\leq i\leq m),\quad t\geq 0.

We call this semiflow {S⁡(t)}t≥0\{S(t)\}_{t\geq 0} the memristive Hindmarsh-Rose neural network semiflow generated by the evolutionary equation (2.1) of the neural network model (1.1).

The next theorem shows that the memristive Hindmarsh-Rose neural network semiflow {S⁡(t)}t≥0\{S(t)\}_{t\geq 0} is a dissipative dynamical system in the state space EE.

4. Exponential Synchronization of the Neural Network

Definition 4.1.

For a model evolutionary equation of a neural network called NW such as (2.1) formulated from the memristive and diffusive Hindmarsh-Rose equations (1.1), we define the asynchronous degree of this neural network in a state space (as a Banach space) ZZ to be

d​e​gs​(NW)=∑1≤i<j≤m{supgi0,gj0∈Z{lim supt→∞‖gi​(t,gi0)−gj​(t,gj0)‖Z}}deg_{s}\,(\text{NW})=\sum_{1\,\leq i\,<j\,\leq\,m}\left\{\sup_{g_{i}^{0},\,g_{j}^{0}\,\in\,Z}\,\left\{\limsup_{t\to\infty}\,\|g_{i}(t;g^{0}_{i})-g_{j}(t;g^{0}_{j})\|_{Z}\right\}\right\}

where gi​(t)g_{i}(t) and gj​(t)g_{j}(t) are any two solutions of (1.1) with the initial states gi0g_{i}^{0} and gj0g_{j}^{0} for two neurons 𝒩i\mathcal{N}_{i} and 𝒩j\mathcal{N}_{j} in the network, respectively. The neural network is said to be asymptotically synchronized if

d​e​gs​(NW)=0.deg_{s}\,(\text{NW})=0.

If the asymptotic convergence to zero of the difference norm for any two neurons in a network admits a uniform exponential rate, then the neural network is called exponentially synchronized.

The following exponential synchronization theorem is the main result of this paper.

Theorem 4.2.

Exponential synchronization in the state space EE occurs for the memristive Hindmarsh-Rose neural network semiflow {S⁡(t)}t≥0\{S(t)\}_{t\geq 0} generated by the weak solutions of the evolutionary equation (2.1), if the network neuron-coupling strength coefficients PP and QQ satisfy the threshold conditions

(4.1) P>1m​[4​a2b+8​β2b​(1+1r)+b16​β2​(1+q2r)+k1​(|c|+γ24​δ)]P>\frac{1}{m}\left[\frac{4a^{2}}{b}+\frac{8\beta^{2}}{b}\left(1+\frac{1}{r}\right)+\frac{b}{16\beta^{2}}\left(1+\frac{q^{2}}{r}\right)+k_{1}\left(|c|+\frac{\gamma^{2}}{4\delta}\right)\right]

and

(4.2) Q≥12​m​[(1+32​β2​k12​γ2b2)+K22​η23​(64​β2​C∗​k12​δ2b2)4],Q\geq\frac{1}{2m}\left[\left(1+\frac{32\beta^{2}k_{1}^{2}\gamma^{2}}{b^{2}}\right)+\frac{K^{2}}{2\eta_{2}^{3}}\left(\frac{64\beta^{2}C^{*}k_{1}^{2}\delta^{2}}{b^{2}}\right)^{4}\right],

(4.20) ‖gi​(t)−gj​(t)‖E2=‖U⁡(t)‖2+‖V⁡(t)‖2+‖W⁡(t)‖2+‖R⁡(t)‖2≤e−κ​t​max⁡{1,C}min⁡{1,C}​‖gi0−gj0‖2=e−κ​tmax⁡{1, 8​β2/b}min⁡{1, 8​β2/b}‖gi0−gj0‖2→0,ast→∞.\begin{split}\|g_{i}(t)-g_{j}(t)\|_{E}^{2}&=\|U(t)\|^{2}+\|V(t)\|^{2}+\|W(t)\|^{2}+\|R(t)\|^{2}\\[5.0pt] &\leq e^{-\kappa\,t}\,\frac{\max\{1,\,C\}}{\min\{1,\,C\}}\,\|g_{i}^{0}-g_{j}^{0}\|^{2}\\ &=e^{-\kappa\,t}\,\frac{\max\{1,\,8\beta^{2}/b\}}{\min\{1,\,8\beta^{2}/b\}}\,\left\|g_{i}^{0}-g_{j}^{0}\right\|^{2}\to 0,\;\;\text{as}\;\,t\to\infty.\end{split}

d​e​gs​(𝒩​𝒲)=∑1≤i<j≤m{supg0∈E{lim supt→∞‖gi​(t)−gj​(t)‖L2​(Ω,ℝ4)2}}=0.deg_{s}(\mathcal{NW})=\sum_{1\,\leq\,i\,<\,j\,\leq\,m}\left\{\sup_{g^{0}\,\in\,E}\,\left\{\limsup_{t\to\infty}\|g_{i}(t)-g_{j}(t)\|^{2}_{L^{2}(\Omega,\mathbb{R}^{4})}\right\}\right\}=0.

Thus the exponential synchronization of this memristive and diffusive Hindmarsh-Rose neural network 𝒩​𝒲\mathcal{NW} modeled by (1.1) in the space EE is proved under the threshold conditions (4.1) and (4.2). The proof is completed. ∎

Conclusions   In this paper, a new model of memristive and diffusive Hindmarsh-Rose neural networks is proposed. This new model features a hybrid system of two partial differential equations with two ordinary differential equations as well as the linear coupling terms in the membrane potential equations and the memristor equations for all neurons.

Dissipative dynamics of the solution semiflow in the basic state space EE and the higher-order state space GG are shown through sophisticated grouping estimates and integral inequality leverage, especially for the highly nonlinear membrane potential PDE with the memductance coupling. It paves the way to explore synchronization of this memristive Hindmarsh-Rose neural network.

The main result is Theorem 4.2, which provides the explicit threshold conditions of the network coupling strengths PP and QQ to ensure an exponential synchronization of the neural network at a uniform convergence rate. The spirit of the entire proof is to tackle and control the higher nonlinearity in the memductance-potential effect by the linear network coupling in the integrable state spaces. Many steps of sharp analysis including Gagliardo-Nirenberg interpolation inequalities are carried out and cohesively grouped. The rigorous mathematical proof methodology in this work can be extended to study more complex neural networks described by hybrid differential equations or other types reaction-diffusion PDE models in a broad scope.
